items.name: Car seat that fits baby's age and size
items.note: Fitted properly, every journey, even short ones.

variants.name: Car seat or booster that fits their age and size

variants.note: Only if you'll drive, hire a car or take taxis when you get there. Some hire firms and taxi services can provide one if you book ahead.

items.name: Travel health insurance with infant cover
items.note: Check your baby is named on the policy and that it covers medical treatment and getting home. A GHIC or EHIC isn't a substitute for insurance.

variants.name: Travel insurance that covers every child

items.name: Baby's passport (if travelling internationally)
items.note: Babies need their own passport. HM Passport Office says to allow up to 3 weeks. Not in the UK? Check your own passport office.

items.name: Vaccination record copy
items.note: Some countries ask for proof of certain vaccinations, such as yellow fever, on arrival. Check your destination on TravelHealthPro.

items.name: Formula + extra supply (if formula-feeding)
items.note: Bring enough for the journey plus extra for delays. Your brand might not be sold where you're going. In the UK, you can take enough for the journey in hand luggage.

items.name: Nursing cover / portable privacy wrap
items.note: Optional. Some parents like one in busy airports and cafés; plenty don't bother.

light.note: A big muslin or a light scarf does the same job.

items.name: Bottles + portable steriliser
items.note: Keep sterilising bottles until baby is 12 months old. A microwave steam bag is handy if your room has a microwave. Follow the pack's instructions.

items.name: A feed ready for take-off and landing
items.note: Breast, bottle or dummy. Sucking and swallowing can help with ear pressure.

variants.note: A drink with a straw or spout, or a snack to chew. Swallowing and chewing can help with ear pressure.

items.name: Plenty of bibs
items.note: More than you'd get through in a day at home.

light.name: Two or three bibs
light.note: A muslin covers the rest. Rinse them in the evening and they’re usually dry by morning.

items.name: Two big muslins
items.note: Probably the hardest-working thing in the bag. One job they shouldn’t do: cover the pram or buggy. The Lullaby Trust says covers can make babies overheat, so use a clip-on sunshade instead.

items.name: Snacks they already know and like
items.note: More than you'd need at home, in case of delays.

items.name: Sippy cup or straw cup
items.note: Spill-resistant, and easier than a bottle once they're drinking water.

items.name: Nappies and wipes for the journey + first day
items.note: You can buy more when you arrive, so there's no need to fill a suitcase.

variants.name: Nappies or pull-ups (if they still use them) and spare pants
variants.note: Accidents happen more when routines change. Pack extra pants in hand luggage.

variants.name: Nappies and wipes for the whole trip
variants.note: For a short trip it's simplest to bring everything, plus a few spares for delays.

items.name: Portable changing mat
items.note: Not every café, train or plane has a changing table.

variants.name: Portable changing mat (if they still use nappies)

light.note: A muslin or small towel can do this job in a pinch.

items.name: Nappy sacks or small rubbish bags
items.note: For dirty nappies and wet clothes when there's no bin in sight.

items.name: A few zip-lock bags
items.note: They weigh nothing and keep the mess away from everything else.

items.name: Spare outfits in your hand luggage
items.note: At least two for baby, and a spare top for you.

light.name: One spare outfit each in your hand luggage
light.note: Plus a spare top for you. If you run out, a big muslin makes a decent toga until you can change.

items.name: Travel potty or fold-up toilet seat
items.note: Handy if they're toilet training. Public toilets are rarely close when you need one.

items.name: A labelled bag of spare clothes for each child
items.note: No digging through one big bag at the worst moment.

items.name: Portable travel cot or book a hotel crib
items.note: If you're using the hotel's cot, ask them to confirm it in writing before you arrive.

items.name: White noise app or portable speaker
items.note: If you use one at home, bring it. A familiar sound can make a new room feel less strange.

light.name: White noise app on your phone
light.note: No need for a separate speaker if your phone can do it.

items.name: Portable blackout blind
items.note: Suction or clip-on blinds fit most windows. Useful for naps in a bright room.

light.note: A dark towel pinned over the curtain rail, well away from the cot, can darken a room for naps.

items.name: Baby's familiar sleep bag
items.note: Something that smells and feels like home.

variants.name: Their own pillowcase or blanket
variants.note: A familiar smell helps a new bed feel like theirs.

variants.name: Baby's familiar sleep bag or swaddle
variants.note: Something that smells and feels like home. If you swaddle, the Lullaby Trust advises stopping once baby shows signs of rolling.

items.name: Their favourite comfort toy (and a backup if you have one)
items.note: Losing it is hard on everyone. Keep it on a clip or in one pocket you always check.

items.name: Nappy rash cream
items.note: Bring the one you already use.

items.name: Antibacterial wipes
items.note: For tray tables, changing mats and sticky hands.

light.note: Baby wipes can do tray tables and sticky hands too.

items.name: Sunhat and stroller sunshade
items.note: The NHS advises keeping babies under 6 months out of direct strong sunlight, so shade is your friend. Ask a pharmacist about sun cream for older babies. Use a clip-on sunshade rather than a muslin or blanket over the pram: the Lullaby Trust says covers can make babies overheat.

items.name: Your child's own medicines, if they take any
items.note: Pack them in hand luggage with the pharmacy label on. At UK airports, liquid medicines over 100ml need a copy of the prescription or a letter from the doctor.

items.name: Infant paracetamol (age-appropriate)
items.note: The NHS says most children over 2 months can have it. Check the dose for their age on the pack, and ask a pharmacist if you're not sure.

variants.name: Children's paracetamol
variants.note: Check the dose for their age on the pack, and ask a pharmacist if you're not sure.
The NHS says babies of 2–3 months can only have paracetamol if they weigh over 4kg and were born after 37 weeks. Ask your GP, pharmacist or health visitor what to bring.

items.name: Children's ibuprofen
items.note: The NHS says most children over 3 months can have it. It may not suit children with asthma or an infection like chickenpox, so ask a pharmacist if you’re not sure.

variants.note: The NHS says babies of 3 to 6 months can have it if they weigh over 5kg, and not for more than 24 hours without speaking to a doctor or pharmacist.

items.name: Digital thermometer
items.note: The NHS recommends a digital thermometer, used under the armpit for children under 5.

items.name: Oral rehydration sachets (ORS)
items.note: A pharmacist can recommend rehydration sachets. If you're worried about a baby under 12 months who's being sick or has diarrhoea, get medical advice straight away (in the UK, call 111).

items.name: Ask a pharmacist what to bring for colds
items.note: Many cough and cold medicines aren’t suitable for young children. The NHS says no decongestants under 6, no honey under 12 months and no aspirin under 16.

items.name: Children's antihistamine, for allergies
items.note: The NHS says chlorphenamine (Piriton) is suitable from age 1, and cetirizine liquid from pharmacies from age 2. Check the pack for their age.

items.name: Travel sickness tablets, if they’re 4 or older
items.note: The NHS says hyoscine (for example Kwells Kids) is for children aged 4 and over. It can cause side effects like confusion in children, so follow the pack and ask a pharmacist.

variants.name: Travel sickness: tips, not tablets, for under-4s
variants.note: The NHS says travel sickness tablets like hyoscine are for children aged 4 and over. For younger children: fresh air, regular breaks, and songs or music instead of screens. If it’s a real problem, ask a pharmacist or GP.

items.name: Your own regular medicines and medical kit
items.note: Inhalers, adrenaline pens, contraception, anything you take daily, plus extra for delays. Keep them in hand luggage. Liquids over 100ml need a copy of the prescription or a doctor’s letter at UK airports; tablets don’t. Some medicines are controlled in other countries, so check with the embassy.

items.name: Pain and fever relief for you
items.note: Paracetamol or ibuprofen. Breastfeeding? The NHS says ibuprofen is thought to be the safest anti-inflammatory, and to check with a GP or midwife before taking paracetamol mixed with other medicines.

items.name: Cold and allergy remedies for you
items.note: Whatever you’d reach for at home. Breastfeeding? The NHS says decongestant tablets or drinks aren’t recommended, and to check with a pharmacist before using nasal sprays, antihistamines or combined cold remedies.

items.name: Travel sickness remedy for you, if you get it
items.note: Some travel sickness medicines are drowsy antihistamines, so they’re not for whoever is driving or looking after the baby alone. Breastfeeding? Ask a pharmacist which suits you.

items.name: A small first-aid kit
items.note: Plasters, antiseptic wipes and tweezers cover most small knocks and splinters.

items.name: Check the airline's infant rules before you book
items.note: Minimum ages, lap fares, bassinets and free baby gear all vary. For example, British Airways takes babies from 48 hours old, easyJet from 14 days and Ryanair from 8 days.

items.name: A change of clothes for you in hand luggage
items.note: Spit-up and spills don't stay on the baby.

items.name: Plan regular breaks out of the car seat
items.note: The Lullaby Trust advises regular breaks on long drives so baby can come out of the seat and stretch, and moving them to a flat sleep space once you arrive.

items.name: Window sunshades for the car
items.note: Keeps direct sun off baby on long drives.

items.name: Rear-facing seat mirror
items.note: So the front-seat adult can glance at baby without turning round.

light.note: Useful if one adult is driving alone with baby. Otherwise easy to leave out.

items.name: Reserve seats near the baby-change or with a table
items.note: A table seat gives you space to feed and change; near the end of the carriage gives you room to walk.

items.name: A few small new toys or books
items.note: New things tend to hold attention for longer. Hand them out one at a time.

light.name: Two or three small new toys or books
light.note: New things hold attention for longer, so a few go a long way. Hand them out one at a time.

items.name: Downloaded shows or music
items.note: Download them before you go. Signal drops on planes, trains and motorways.

items.name: A small backpack they carry themselves
items.note: Let them choose a few toys and a snack. It gives them a job and something to look forward to.

items.name: A grown-up for each lap baby
items.note: Each adult can only hold one baby on their lap. With two under-2s, book a second adult or a seat for one of them.

items.name: A job for older siblings
items.note: Snack keeper, ticket holder or music chooser. It gives them something to do.

items.name: A bag within reach, not in the boot
items.note: Nappies, wipes, snacks, drinks and a spare outfit, so you don’t have to unpack the boot in a lay-by.

items.name: Sick bags, an old towel and wipes
items.note: Car sickness can come on fast. The NHS suggests fresh air, looking ahead at the horizon and breaking up long journeys, and talking or singing rather than screens.

items.name: Water, snacks and a blanket for hold-ups
items.note: Enough for everyone if you’re stuck in traffic for a while.

items.name: Phone charger and holder
items.note: For maps, white noise and calls, without anyone holding the phone.

items.name: One small bag for your seat
items.note: Big bags go in the rack. Keep feeds, nappies, snacks and a change of clothes with you.

items.name: Tickets and seat reservations on your phone, with a screenshot
items.note: Signal can drop just when the ticket inspector arrives.

items.name: Baby milk, food and medicines in one easy-to-reach bag
items.note: At UK airports you can take enough baby milk, food and sterilised water for the journey, even over 100ml. Breast milk is allowed in containers up to 2 litres; formula and baby food only if your baby is travelling. Staff may open containers to check them.

variants.name: Snacks, drinks and medicines in one easy-to-reach bag
variants.note: Keep them easy to reach at security. At UK airports, essential medicines over 100ml are allowed in hand luggage with a copy of the prescription or a doctor’s letter. Staff may open containers to check them.

items.name: Passports and boarding passes in one pocket
items.note: Everyone’s, including the children’s. You’ll be asked for them at check-in, security and the gate, often with your hands full.

items.name: Layers and a light blanket
items.note: Easy to add or take off as the cabin warms up or cools down.

items.name: Bags or covers for the stroller and car seat
items.note: Keeps the parts together and stops them getting grubby in the hold.

light.note: Nice for keeping things clean, but your gear will be fine without.

items.name: Lightweight stroller
items.note: Compact and easy to fold one-handed.

variants.name: Lightweight, foldable stroller
variants.note: Ask at check-in whether you can use it to the gate. Some airlines, like British Airways, return slimline pushchairs to the aircraft door at certain airports.

items.name: Baby carrier / sling
items.note: Hands-free and better than a stroller in crowds or cobblestones.

variants.name: A carrier or light stroller for tired legs

variants.note: Handy on stairs and busy platforms, so you’re not carrying a stroller and bags at the same time.

jobs: A nap spot on the go
Hands free for bags and tickets

items.name: Nappy bag with packing cubes
items.note: Separate cubes for feeding, changing and sleep, so things are quick to find.

variants.name: Day bag with snacks, wipes and a spare outfit

light.note: Any backpack you already have will do.

items.name: Travel wash or a place with a washing machine
items.note: On longer trips it's lighter to wash than to pack for every day.

light.name: Plan to do a wash
light.note: Packing for half the trip and washing once is lighter than packing for every day.

items.name: Earphones for you
items.note: For when baby finally sleeps.

items.name: Double stroller, or a stroller plus a carrier
items.note: Keeps your hands free for bags and boarding passes.
